hints: Focus on the two functional groups in the same molecule, an alcohol and a carboxylic acid, and what happens when they meet with warm concentrated acid.
Count the atoms that will join to make the ring, the O from $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ must bond to the $\text{C=O}$ carbon of $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ with loss of water.
Check where the $\text{C=C}$ double bond and the $\text{CH}_2$ group end up in the 5-membered lactone, then match that pattern to the skeletal drawings.
walkthrough:
**Spot the two reacting groups**

Look at $\text{CH}_2(\text{OH})\text{CH=CHCO}_2\text{H}$. At one end you have a primary alcohol, at the other end a carboxylic acid.

Warm concentrated sulfuric acid removes water and encourages esterification:
$$\text{R-OH + HOOC-R'} \rightarrow \text{R-OOC-R' + H}_2\text{O}$$

**Form the intramolecular ester**

Because both groups are in the same molecule, the ester forms internally to give a cyclic ester, called a lactone.

Join the alcoholic O to the carboxylic C:
$$\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH-C(=O)-OH} \rightarrow \text{ring: -O-CH}_2\text{-CH=CH-C(=O)-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Check the ring size and unsaturation**

Count round the new ring: O (1), $\text{CH}_2$ (2), CH (3), CH (4), C=O (5). It is a 5-membered unsaturated lactone.

The $\text{CH}_2$ stays next to the ring O, the $\text{C=C}$ stays in the middle of the chain, and the $\text{C=O}$ stays next to the ring O on the other side. That matches structure C, furan-2(5H)-one.

options.A: This shows a ketone ($\text{C=O}$ outside an all-carbon part) plus an enol ether ($\text{C=C-O}$). Our product must be an ester inside the ring ($\text{O-C=O}$), not a separate ketone, so the carbonyl is in the wrong place.
options.B: This is also a 5-membered lactone but the positions are swapped. It puts the $\text{C=O}$ next to $\text{CH}_2$ and the O next to $\text{CH}$, which would need the OH to be on the alkene carbon. Our OH is on the $\text{CH}_2$ group, so this connectivity is backwards.
options.C: Correct. The ring O is joined to $\text{CH}_2$ on one side and to $\text{C=O}$ on the other side, with the $\text{CH=CH}$ double bond preserved between them. This is exactly the intramolecular ester from $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH=CHCOOH}$ minus water.
options.D: This shows two $\text{C=O}$ groups in the ring, like a cyclic anhydride. We only have one carboxylic acid carbon, so we can only make one ester $\text{C=O}$. This trap comes from miscounting oxygens or confusing esterification with anhydride formation.
